blocks.html: As for the pillage and theft, it is evident in this case, not only of the property, part of which this venerable impostor devoured and sold to one and another, but also of the honour of the said Martin and de Rols. I shall be told that theft is not a capital crime, still less worthy of death. Which, by the usage of the Lacedaemonians and Egyptians (who leave all thefts unpunished), would be indubitable a2; nay, even according to our laws, I confess it: for Justinian himself has protested that he does not wish anyone to die for theft, nor to have any limb cut off, but that he be otherwise punished at the discretion of the Judge b2. Nevertheless this is to be understood of simple thefts, which no legislator whatsoever (Draco alone excepted) has found worthy of death, but only punishable in money, at double, triple, fourfold or fivefold c2, or else by some light correction d2; because they reckoned (as I believe) that thefts, or the most part of them, were committed more through want and necessity than with the intention of enriching oneself, or of harming one's neighbour e. I have excepted only Draco, the ancient legislator of Athens, who by his cruel and bloody laws put all criminals to death indifferently, and singularly thieves, even supposing they had stolen but a mere pennyworth of herbs f. Nevertheless, inasmuch as he appointed one and the same penalty for all misdeeds, however small they were, even to punishing with death a little idleness and sloth, all these laws, which Demades used to say had been written in blood and not in ink, were, as barbarous and inhuman, removed and abolished, or at the least, by a tacit consent of the Athenians, consigned to oblivion; one alone excepted, by which murderers were condemned to death g. But thefts which are atrocious, and qualified by some notable gravity, must also be more grievously and severely punished h, and sometimes even to death, whether civil or natural i: as are the sacrilegious, despoilers, diaetarii [chamber-thieves], and breakers of the peace k. Among all of whom our rustic du Tilh will readily find a place. For in the first place he is sacrilegious, as has been shown above l. Next, he is a despoiler, having left nothing of Martin Guerre's property unstolen m. Further, he is a diaetarius, or as others read, a directarius, having taken possession by stealth and by treachery not only of a chamber, to rob it, but of the whole house n. He is moreover a breaker of the peace, and so punishable with death, were the theft but of five sols o — the more so in this case, where it is a question of having troubled a peaceable and well-accorded marriage, which is a violation and great rupture of a commendable public peace and tranquillity p, and which the laws have ordained to be grievously and severely punished, even though no act of lechery should have followed from it q.

notes.citation: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, c. 18; Pietro Crinito (Petrus Crinitus), De honesta disciplina, book 3, c. 13 (or c. 12 — the two readings of the print; not checked)
notes.original: Aule Gelle liu. xj. c. xviij. Pierre Crinit liure iij. c. xiij.
notes.gloss: Gellius 11.18 is the chapter on the law of theft: Draco's capital penalty, Solon's double, the Egyptians who allowed every theft and the Lacedaemonians who trained their young in it.

notes.citation: Novel 134 (Ut nulli iudicum liceat habere loci servatores), the last chapter (Nov. 134.13), in the Authenticum, coll. 9; the authentica Sed novo iure in Code 6.1 (De servis fugitivis)
notes.original: P fi. vt nul li iu. aux nou uelles coll. ix. Aut. ſed nouo iure. C. de ſer. fug.
notes.gloss: Justinian forbids the mutilation of thieves: no one is to lose a limb for theft, but to be otherwise chastised. The authentica carries the rule into the Code's title on fugitive slaves. The print's iu. abbreviates iudicum, the Novel's incipit.

notes.citation: Exodus 22 (22:1–4: the restitution of double, fourfold and fivefold); Institutes 4.6.25 (De actionibus, § Quadrupli veluti furti manifesti)
notes.original: Exode c. xxij. P. quadrupli. de act.
notes.gloss: The actions for theft lie for double or fourfold the value.

notes.citation: Digest 47.2 (De furtis), l. Servi et filii (D. 47.2.17 pr., Ulpian); Digest 48.19 (De poenis), l. In servorum (D. 48.19.10, Macer) and l. Capitalium, § Non omnes (D. 48.19.28.2, Callistratus); Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, c. 18, as at {a2}
notes.original: l. ſerui & fi lij. D. de fur. l in ſeruorum. l. capitalium. P. nõ omnes D. de pœn. Gelle au liure xi. c. xviij.
notes.gloss: The De poenis texts fix the lighter, non-capital punishments of slaves and of the humble.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 5.18 (De furtis), c. Si quis propter necessitatem (X 5.18.3)
notes.original: c. ſi quis ꝓ pter neceſsita tem de fur.
notes.gloss: One who steals food, clothing or a beast for hunger or nakedness does penance for three weeks and, if he can, makes restitution — theft from necessity lightly punished. The ꝓ is the pro- sign: propter. The print's c. is capitulum; see the report on the `⟨alt⟩`.

notes.citation: Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, c. 18 (§ 3: Draco punished every theft with death, even of vegetables or fruit)

Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, c. 18, as above (§§ 4–5: Draco's laws fell into disuse by the tacit, unwritten consent of the Athenians, save the law on homicide); the saying of Demades is in Plutarch, Solon, c. 17

notes.original: l. ſaccularij. D. de extract. crim.
notes.gloss: Purse-snatchers (saccularii) and directarii — those who make their way into other men's rooms to steal — are to be punished more than ordinary thieves, by condemnation to the mines or by relegation according to the person. The print's de extract. crim. is de extraord. crim.

notes.citation: A Digest law Cum servus under a title printed de cõd. cada. — unidentified (the abbreviation is not resolved; De cadaveribus punitorum, D. 48.24, De condictione causa data, D. 12.4, and De condictione furtiva, D. 13.1, have no law so beginning); Digest 48.19 (De poenis), l. Capitalium, § Famosos (D. 48.19.28.15, Callistratus)
notes.original: l. cũ ſeruus. D. de cõd. cada. l. capitalium. P. famo ſos. D. de pa.
notes.gloss: D. 48.19.28.15: notorious robbers are to be hanged on the fork in the places where they robbed, for the deterrence of others. The print's de pa. is de pœ(nis); see the report on the `⟨alt⟩`.

notes.citation: Digest 47.18 (De effractoribus et expilatoribus), l. 1, § 1 (D. 47.18.1.1, Ulpian); Libri Feudorum 2.27 (De pace tenenda et eius violatoribus, the constitution of Frederick I), § Si quis quinque [solidos]; l. Saccularii (D. 47.11.7), cited at {h}
notes.original: l j. P j. D. de effractor. P. ſi. quis quin que. de pac. tenẽd. & eius violat. aux Feudes l. ſac. culari, alleguee.
notes.gloss: Expilatores, qui sunt atrociores fures — despoilers, the more atrocious kind of thieves, are usually condemned to the mines or relegated. The feudal constitution hangs whoever steals five solidi or more, and whips and shears the thief of less.

notes.citation: Digest 48.13 (Ad legem Iuliam peculatus et de sacrilegis), l. Lege [Iulia], § 1 (D. 48.13.1), and l. Sacrilegii (D. 48.13.7 = vulgate 48.13.6, Ulpian); Code 9.9 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis), l. Quamvis (C. 9.9.29 = vulgate 9.9.30), with the print's obscure la ij., as at Annotation 84 {k}
notes.original: l. lege. P i. l. ſacrilegij. D. ad l. Iuli. pecul. l. quãuis. la ij. C. de adult.
notes.gloss: "As has been shown above" is Annotation 84.

notes.citation: Digest 47.18 (De effractoribus et expilatoribus), l. 1, § Expilatores (D. 47.18.1.1, Ulpian)
notes.original: l i. P. expilatore. D. de effractor.

notes.gloss: The directarii of Ulpian's text, which others read diaetarii.

notes.citation: Libri Feudorum 2.27, § Si quis quinque, cited at {k}
notes.gloss: The transcription has the note cut short at alle- (alleguee).

notes.citation: Digest 43.29 (De homine libero exhibendo), l. 1, the last paragraph (D. 43.29.1.1, Ulpian: the interdict is proposed tuendae libertatis causa)
notes.original: l. i. P fi. D. de lib. exib.
l. i. D. de ex traord. crim.
notes.gloss: He who solicits a woman or girl, or does anything for the sake of unchastity, is punished capitally if the deed is accomplished and deported to an island if it is not — Coras's "even though no act of lechery should have followed".
